qs.q: An older adult undergoes a major vascular catheterization procedure and subsequently develops acute renal failure accompanied by livedo reticularis and peripheral eosinophilia. What is the most likely renal pathology?
o: Atheroembolic renal disease caused by cholesterol crystals breaking off plaques
Typical hemolytic uremic syndrome caused by Shiga-like bacterial toxins
Fibromuscular dysplasia affecting the main renal artery in younger women
Malignant nephrosclerosis resulting from a blood pressure over 200/120 mmHg
qs.e: Atheroembolic renal disease occurs when cholesterol crystals break off from aortic plaques to block small vessels, typically triggered by vascular procedures. This differs from HUS, which is triggered by bacterial enteritis in children.

ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Renal pathology covers acute and chronic kidney disease, each with distinct causes, clinical clues, and investigations. Understanding the underlying mechanisms helps clinicians decide when to treat, dialyse, or refer.

sections.p: The kidneys filter blood, reabsorb needed substances, and excrete waste. Pathology arises when this balance is disrupted, leading to acute or chronic dysfunction.
b: Acute kidney injury (AKI) is sudden, reversible if treated early.
Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is progressive, often silent until advanced.

sections.p: Glomerular filtration, tubular reabsorption, and secretion maintain fluid, electrolytes, and acid-base balance. Hormones like EPO, renin, and PTH modulate red cell production and mineral metabolism.
b: Filtration rate depends on glomerular pressure and permeability.
Tubular cells reabsorb glucose, sodium, and water; secrete potassium and hydrogen.

sections.p: Renal function is regulated by neurohormonal systems: sympathetic tone, renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, and antidiuretic hormone. Disturbances in these pathways contribute to pathology.
b: Angiotensin II constricts efferent arterioles, raising GFR but increasing sodium reabsorption.
ADH concentrates urine; excess leads to water retention.

sections.p: AKI arises from pre‑renal (hypovolemia), intrinsic (tubular necrosis, glomerulonephritis), or post‑renal (obstruction). CKD results from long‑term damage: diabetes, hypertension, infections, or toxins.
b: Pre‑renal AKI shows low fractional excretion of sodium (<1%).
Intrinsic AKI often shows high FENa (>2%) and muddy brown casts.

sections.p: Early recognition of AKI prevents progression to CKD. CKD management focuses on slowing decline, treating anemia, mineral bone disease, and preparing for dialysis.
b: Oliguria, rising creatinine, and hyperkalemia signal urgent care.
Anemia in CKD is due to low erythropoietin; treat with EPO analogues.

sections.p: In low‑resource settings, focus on clinical signs, simple urine dipstick, and basic labs.
b: If a test is unavailable, use bedside creatinine and urine output to guide management.

t.b: Assess filtration; rising values indicate AKI or CKD.
Detect casts, protein, and hematuria; muddy brown casts suggest ATN.
Hyperkalemia risks arrhythmia; hypocalcemia and hyperphosphatemia indicate CKD.
Quantify proteinuria; >300 mg/day suggests glomerular disease.

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, support renal function, and monitor complications. Drug choices consider renal clearance and side‑effect profile.
b: Pre‑renal AKI: volume repletion with isotonic saline.
Intrinsic AKI: stop nephrotoxins, consider dialysis if severe.
CKD: control blood pressure with ACE inhibitors or ARBs, manage anemia with EPO, treat mineral bone disease with phosphate binders and vitamin D.

sections.p: Acute tubular necrosis can mimic post‑renal obstruction; nephrotic syndrome may be mistaken for acute glomerulonephritis.
b: Both can present with proteinuria and edema; imaging distinguishes obstruction.

sections.p: Serum creatinine may be normal early in AKI; low urine sodium can occur in intrinsic AKI if diuretics used.
b: In CKD, serum creatinine may be normal until >50% loss of function.

sections.p: Remember the mnemonic RAIN: Renal, Acute, Intrinsic, Nephron. Use FENa to differentiate pre‑renal from intrinsic AKI.
b: In CKD, stage G3b or higher warrants referral for dialysis planning.

whenToSeekHelp: Rapid rise in serum creatinine (>0.3 mg/dL in 48h)

faq.q: What is the difference between AKI and CKD?
faq.a: AKI is sudden, potentially reversible; CKD is gradual, progressive, and often irreversible.
It helps distinguish pre‑renal (low FENa) from intrinsic (high FENa) AKI.

faq.q: How does anemia develop in CKD?
faq.a: Reduced erythropoietin production by damaged kidneys leads to decreased red cell production.
